comparator.name: BA European Languages and Cultures — German major, European Language and Society profile
comparator.route: German major language — European Language and Society profile
comparator.sourceNotes: The normalized target is the generic 180-EC European Languages and Cultures bachelor. The current official curriculum requires one major language and specialization in one or two of three profiles from Year 2. No profile or major language is substantively more representative of the generic degree. The European Language and Society profile and German major are therefore instantiated through the official-order tie-break: Language and Society is listed first among the profiles, and German is listed first among the major-language options. The pathway preserves the formal 60-EC structure of each year, the 10-EC restricted elective, the 30-EC minor, the 10-EC thesis and every language-specific component without inventing optional content.

questionsApplications.label: How do language, media and communication shape identity and power in European societies?
How do literature and cultural expression represent similarities and differences across Europe?
How have political institutions and social change shaped modern Europe and its future challenges?

alternatives.concept: Study language as a social and cultural practice through introductory Dutch, stylistics, psycholinguistics, rhetoric and communication, then connect it to European identity, literature, media, sociology, social change and EU politics. This related-fields route has no German proficiency sequence or German-language academic work.

How do language, media and communication shape identity and power in European societies?
alternatives.labelRationale: The curriculum combines seven language and communication courses, literature and media, sociology, European history and EU politics. The label reflects that balance and does not imply German proficiency.

alternatives.concept: Study how literary, rhetorical and media forms create cultural meaning and express identity and power, combining textual interpretation, stylistics, psycholinguistics, intercultural communication, film and multimodal production. European and German-language depth remain explicit gaps.
basisLabels: Language proficiency, language-and-society analysis, multilingual communication and language-specific academic work

European politics, institutions, social change and contemporary challenges
How do literature and cultural expression represent similarities and differences across Europe?
alternatives.labelRationale: The completed route concentrates on literature, stylistics, rhetoric, psycholinguistics, film, media and cultural identity; it does not claim German proficiency.
alternatives.distinctnessRationale: Five courses / 37.5 EC differ in each direction. The closest route’s Dutch, EU politics, modern sociology, social movements and applied civic research give way to introductory literary study, major literary traditions, imperial history, myth and advanced adaptation study.

alternatives.concept: Study modern European history, political institutions, international relations, migration, civil society, identity, conflict, environmental movements and public culture as a related social-science and humanities route. Preserve German-language proficiency and language-specific study as explicit gaps.
basisLabels: European cultures, identities, literature, text, media and comparative cultural analysis

How have political institutions and social change shaped modern Europe and its future challenges?
alternatives.labelRationale: The curriculum is led by European history, politics, international relations, sociology, conflict and public culture and does not present itself as European Languages and Cultures.
alternatives.distinctnessRationale: The politics route differs from the closest route by ten courses / 75 EC and from the culture route by ten courses / 75 EC. It replaces Dutch, stylistics, psycholinguistics and much literary/media production with political philosophy, comparative politics, international relations, historical research, conflict and critical-information analysis.

alternativeSelection.assessment: Three complete and genuinely different related-fields programmes are defensible: language, culture and society; literature, media and cultural identity; and modern European politics and social change. All three pass the pairwise 30-EC floor. The eight language-direction rows were assessed separately and remain infeasible because UCR lacks cumulative proficiency study; the maximum of three alternatives is reached.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: Both analyse language and society; UCR focuses on stylistics and meaning rather than German proficiency.
Both examine identities through media and culture; UCR is a general media course.
Both develop narrative interpretation and production; UCR focuses on documentary.
Both introduce textual and cultural interpretation.
Both introduce the study of modern Europe; UCR uses historical analysis rather than an integrated programme gateway.
Both develop academic inquiry and qualitative interpretation.
Both examine European institutions and political decision-making.
Both analyse language, culture and society within modern social change; UCR is general sociology.
Both examine society, institutions and public life through advanced theory.
Both examine collective action and contemporary social change.
Both introduce comparative political analysis of European societies.

notes.text: Groningen European Languages and Cultures combines cumulative major-language proficiency with language-specific study and one or two formal profiles. UCR can build coherent related programmes in language and society, culture and literature, or European politics and society, but these are not European-language degree pathways.

UCR offers introductory Dutch but no German course and no cumulative proficiency sequence in any European language, language-specific profile modules or thesis in the major language. Psycholinguistics, stylistics, literature, media, history and politics remain related disciplinary perspectives rather than substitutes.
